rounds.name: Online Assessment Round
rounds.description: The online assessment was conducted on the HackerRank platform, consisting of 36 questions to be solved in 120 minutes. The test covered a mix of topics including Computer Networks, Operating Systems, SQL, Logical Reasoning, Probability, and Puzzles, along with two coding problems based on Tree and Dynamic Programming (DP). There were also multiple SQL query-based questions that tested basic to intermediate understanding of joins, aggregate functions, and constraints. The non-technical sections focused on logical reasoning and quantitative aptitude, including probability-based word problems and short analytical puzzles.

tips.text: Always keep a smile. It instantly lightens the mood and helps the interview flow more naturally. Even if you’re nervous, a calm and pleasant expression makes a big difference.
Don’t panic. Once you start panicking, it affects how you think and respond. Take a breath before answering it’s okay to pause for a moment and gather your thoughts.

Never lie. If you don’t know an answer, start with “I think…” and try to reason it out. But if the interviewer keeps digging deeper, be honest and admit you’re not sure. They appreciate honesty more than guessing blindly.
For DSA, I’d recommend NeetCode 75 it’s concise and covers all core patterns. But don’t just focus on DSA. Prepare OOPs, SQL, and core CS topics like OS and Networking too.
For Aptitude, try solving from InterviewBit’s aptitude section, it’s straightforward and helps you build consistency.
Be thorough with your resume. Know every line of it and never include something you can’t explain in detail.
Luck plays its part. Sometimes it’s about the panel you get or the questions asked but solid preparation and the right mindset always tilt luck in your favor.

tips.text: DO NOT UNDERESTIMATE APTITUDE – IT IS JUST AS IMPORTANT AS YOUR DSA AND PLAYS A CRUCIAL ROLE IN GETTING SHORTLISTED FOR THE NEXT ROUND.
Be careful and confident while introducing and explaining yourself. Interviewers can easily sense if you’re faking something. Authenticity matters.
This round was heavily project-focused. It tested how well you can present your work, defend your choices, and explain your technology stack.
Be 100% sure about what you have built. If it’s on your resume, you should be able to explain it thoroughly.
First impressions matter, but consistency seals it. Even if the interviewer seems disinterested, maintain energy and confidence.
Projects are your strongest asset – be ready to explain them multiple times, even on paper, and defend your choices.
Be thorough with basics in C++, SQL, and core concepts – they often act as filters.
Stay updated with AI/ML advancements – it shows genuine interest in your field.
Maintain a Strong CGPA A CGPA ≥ 7.5 is mandatory – aim higher to stay safe.
Know Your Resume Inside Out Be ready to explain every detail of your projects and experiences. Do not fake anything – honesty is valued more than exaggeration.
Focus on Aptitude Aptitude is a crucial shortlisting factor – give it equal importance as DSA.
Practice DSA Daily Strengthen your problem-solving skills. Also, build an understanding of how DSA concepts are applied in real-world scenarios.
Master CS Fundamentals (priority order) OOPS == DBMS → OS == CCN These topics form the backbone of most technical interviews.
Showcase All-Round Skills Highlight leadership qualities and extra-curricular activities. Companies value candidates who are not just technically strong but also versatile.
Believe in Yourself Confidence, consistency, and self-belief are key to overcoming rejections and moving forward.

tips.text: Communication should be top notch; you don’t have to know everything in tech but can’t lack in communication and self-confidence.

Get a good sleep one night before interview. In majority cases, OA shortlist is released one night before interview. I’d strongly suggest to get a good sleep rather than preparing all night for interview, I’ve regretted it every time.
Finally, be patient. This was my 10th interview; I’ve failed 9 company interviews before ofss.

I’ve seen people better than me getting into worse companies that came early, and also people less capable than me getting into better companies. There are a lot of uncertainties, and be prepared to handle them.

rounds.name: OA
rounds.description: The test was for 95 minutes. It started off with 32 MCQs covering stuff like LLMs, Cloud, basic aptitude, api knowledge and some core tech subjects. There were also a few graph-related ones like articulation points and DFS traversal. After that, there were 2 coding questions (everyone had different sets).

questions.text: We were given a list of requests, each having a user ID and a timestamp. The task was to decide whether each request should be allowed or not. A request could only be allowed if the user had made fewer than k requests in the last 1-minute window. Example: n = 3, user = [1, 1, 1], timestamp = [6, 10, 65], k = 2 Output → [1, 1, 0]

Two interns had to complete n tasks. Out of these, the first intern had to do exactly k tasks and the second intern would do the rest. Each intern had rewards for every task, and we had to maximize the total reward. Example: n = 5, reward_1 = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1], reward_2 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 3 Output → 21

rounds.name: 1st Technical Interview
rounds.description: For me it was a cakewalk — mine lasted only about 10–15 minutes (I think being the last one actually helped). I heard other people’s interviews went on for 30 minutes to an hour. They started by asking me for a short intro and then jumped straight into four basic DSA questions... After that they asked what my primary coding language was and whether I’d done development in Java. I was honest and said I hadn’t. Then we moved on to REST APIs — I had to write a basic fetch request, explain query parameters and how they work, and discuss alternatives to query params. Finally they asked a basic SQL join syntax and that wrapped up my first interview.

rounds.name: 2nd Tech+ HR
rounds.description: This was the techno-HR round. Five minutes after I finished Round 1, I was called for Round 2 — this one was taken by one of the directors of OFSS (the same person who did the PPT), so paying attention during the talk actually helped. This round was totally resume-driven — no DSA, SQL, or puzzles. The interviewer went through my resume and then we started with a short intro. He was super friendly and asked about my JEE journey, why I chose SPIT instead of an IIT/NIT, and why I went into engineering — those are open-ended, so be honest. He asked about my primary coding language and what made me pick it, then asked me to explain a recent project and drilled a few follow-ups. He also asked about my positions of responsibility — what my role was and how I balanced it with academics. Since I’d been the marketing head, he gave me a Shark-Tank style task: imagine he was Jack Ma with 200 million to invest — pitch one of your crowdfunding projects and convince him to invest. At first I started explaining the project, then realized I needed to market it — so I switched to a pitch mode and that worked out well; the interviewer seemed happy. He then asked some Java basics: what the import statement does, the difference between interfaces and abstraction (I gave examples), packages in Java, and to explain the static and final keywords. At the end he asked if I had any questions. From the PPT I remembered they mentioned AI models, so I asked whether Oracle (or the company) was building in-house AI models and how those models are affecting the company — I also asked his view on whether AI is a boon or a curse for people in tech. We wrapped up, shook hands, and I left. It lasted for around 35- 40 mins.

rounds.description: This one was more of a formality — the HR even mentioned it wasn’t really an “interview,” just a basic conversation. She asked me how my day had been so far, then a few simple things like my nationality and whether I was open to relocation. After that, she gave me a small situation-based question: “Imagine you’re a team lead and a conflict breaks out between two high-temper teammates — how would you handle it?” I answered confidently about keeping calm, listening to both sides, and resolving it fairly. She seemed satisfied with my response and told me to wait for the results once everyone else was done.

tips.text: Since you could navigate between questions, it’s better to attempt the coding ones first (they weren’t too hard) and then move on to MCQs. Completing both coding questions was super important to get shortlisted for interviews.
pay close attention during the PPT, because it really helps when you want to ask relevant questions later.

Some students were grilled pretty hard on Java — things like file handling, inline functions, REST APIs, and Postman. A Postman question was “How would you test two APIs where the output of one is the input of the other?” — so make sure you can explain chaining API calls clearly. Also, those who had knowledge of Spring / Spring Boot were questioned in much more detail, so be thorough if you mention it on your resume.Some candidates were asked about MongoDb and were asked to write basic fetch and how to save on db queries and connections queries.
be yourself, be confident, and know your resume inside out.
Communication skills and confidence are key and be you, be honest.
Always take a pause and understand if the interviewer is keeping pace with you.
Try hard, think out loud, ask for hints if you’re stuck.
If you need a minute to think or frame an answer, ask the interviewer for the same.
Stay confident, a partially correct answer with 100% confidence is better than a fully correct answer with 50% confidence.
Always give examples while explaining stuff wherever possible, preferably something relatable.
Keep questions ready for the interviewer, they always ask if you have any questions for them, never say no here.
Be attentive during the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) as you’ll get enough content to ask relevant questions.
Your introduction should be short and to the point, and mention things you are good at as the interviewer may lead the discussion based on them.
Be well versed with your resume from top to bottom.
Don’t just focus on DSA completely, make projects (do them yourself and try to participate in hackathons as winning is not important, the learning is) and have internship experience too.
Always have a smile on your face and be interactive with your interviewer, even while solving something share your thought process.
Interviewers are not just assessing your technical skills, they are also assessing your mindset and your approach.

Don’t follow previous interview experiences blindly, as those are from people who got selected but those who didn’t may have had completely different experiences, so be confident in your strong points.
always expect the unexpected.
be confident in what you know, and don’t let external factors shake your confidence.
You need to be patient, learn from your failures, and put in more effort the next time.
always keep a smile, keep working hard, and stay strong.
